question: What limits the speed and cost of AI model inference, and which model-level and service-level techniques address those limits?
contributions: Defines inference bottlenecks (compute-bound vs memory bandwidth-bound) and the metrics TTFT, TPOT, throughput, goodput, MFU and MBU.
Gives a short overview of AI accelerators (compute, memory hierarchy, power).
Surveys model-level optimization (compression, speculative and parallel decoding, attention and KV cache, kernels and compilers).
Surveys service-level optimization (batching, prefill/decode disaggregation, prompt caching, parallelism).

limits: Prices, batch-API discounts, MFU benchmarks and hardware specs are as of the book's writing (2024) and have dated.
The author says the techniques are 'still evolving' and the examples illustrate what solutions might look like.
The PyTorch case study gives no information on output quality after quantization and speculative decoding.
Hardware design is out of scope; the chapter covers model and service levels only.
Throughput and speedup figures are mostly quoted from vendors and other papers, not measured by the author.
Equations for MBU and the numeric values in Figures 9-5 and 9-14 are not in the extracted text (equations render as trailing fragments; figures are images).
practices: Identify whether a workload is compute-bound or memory bandwidth-bound before choosing an optimization (Computational bottlenecks).
Send work without strict latency needs to batch APIs for about 50% lower cost (Online and batch inference APIs).
Report latency in percentiles (p50, p90, p95, p99), not averages, and plot TTFT against input length (Latency, TTFT, and TPOT).
Count input and output throughput separately and compare inference servers by cost per request (Throughput and goodput).
Track goodput (requests meeting the SLO) rather than raw throughput alone (Throughput and goodput).
Do not use nvidia-smi GPU utilization as an efficiency metric; use MFU and MBU (Utilization, MFU, and MBU).
If workloads are compute-bound look for chips with more FLOP/s; if memory-bound look for more bandwidth and memory (Selecting accelerators).
Use weight-only quantization as the default first step because it is easy and effective (Model compression).
Use speculative decoding when decode is memory bandwidth-bound; it makes less sense if MFU is already maxed out (Speculative decoding, footnote).
Use continuous batching so finished responses return immediately and new requests fill the slot (Batching).
Disaggregate prefill and decode onto separate instances to improve volume within latency targets (Decoupling prefill and decode).
Use prompt caching for long, overlapping system prompts, long documents and multi-turn chat (Prompt caching).
For strict latency, prefer replica parallelism over pipeline parallelism (Parallelism).
Evaluate quality after optimizations, since providers' optimizations can change model behavior (Inference Optimization, Figure 9-8).

terms.definition: Tasks whose time-to-complete is determined by the computation needed for the tasks.
Tasks constrained by the data transfer rate within the system, such as the speed of data movement between memory and processors.
The number of arithmetic operations per byte of memory access.
Time to first token: how quickly the first token is generated after users send a query; corresponds to the prefill step.
Time per output token: how quickly each output token is generated after the first token.
A metric measuring time to the first token users see, used when models generate hidden intermediate steps.
The number of output tokens per second an inference service can generate across all users and requests.
The number of requests per second that satisfies the SLO.
Model FLOP/s Utilization: the ratio of the observed throughput (tokens/s) relative to the theoretical maximum throughput of a system operating at peak FLOP/s.
Model Bandwidth Utilization: the percentage of achievable memory bandwidth used.
Uses a faster but less powerful draft model to generate a sequence of tokens, which are then verified by the target model.
Like speculative decoding, but draft tokens are copied from the input instead of generated by a model.
The cache that stores key and value vectors for reuse across decoding steps.
Code optimized for a specific chip.
Converting a model script into a language compatible with the target hardware.
Static groups a fixed number of inputs; dynamic adds a maximum time window; continuous returns completed responses immediately and adds new requests in their place.
Stores overlapping prompt segments for reuse so they are processed once; also called context cache or prefix cache.
Intra-operator parallelism: tensors involved in an operator are partitioned across multiple devices.
Dividing a model's computation into stages and assigning each stage to a different device.
The input sequence itself is split across different devices to be processed separately.
Operators needed for the entire input are split across machines (e.g., attention on one, feedforward on another).
